paragraphs.text: I think my city should adopt a carbon price, and honestly I changed my mind on this over the semester. At first it just sounded like another tax that would make gas and electricity cost more for people like my family who are already kind of stretched. But the more I read the more I realized the whole point is that putting a price on pollution makes the people doing the polluting actually pay for it instead of everybody else dealing with the smog and the heat.
A well-designed carbon price doesn't just raise costs; it sends a clear market signal that rewards cleaner choices and lets households and businesses decide for themselves how to cut emissions.
The part that worries me is fairness, because a flat fee hits lower-income families harder than rich ones.
As the Climate Leadership Council notes, "a carbon dividend that returns the revenue directly to citizens would leave the majority of American families better off financially."
So if my city did this, I'd want the money handed back to residents as a rebate instead of disappearing into some random budget line.
Ultimately, adopting a carbon price is less about punishment and more about aligning everyday incentives with the kind of cleaner, healthier city we actually want to live in.
It won't fix everything overnight, but at least it would push us in the right direction, and that's better than sitting around doing nothing while the summers keep getting hotter.
